articles.title_orig: Italy’s PM deploys troops as nation faces widespread strikes and port blockades
articles.title_zh: Italy’s PM deploys troops as nation faces widespread strikes and port blockades
articles.content_orig:
ROME — Tens of thousands of people were getting ready to take to the streets of Rome, Milan and other Italian cities Friday as part of nationwide demonstrations against the cost of living and high military spending.
After several weeks of violent protests in Italy and throughout Europe , more widespread disruption is expected after the Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) and other trade unions called on workers in both the public and private sectors to strike and protest.
The demonstrations in Italy appear to have been partly inspired by those in France , where some of the worst rioting in decades erupted in cities across the country after student protests about the state of education in the country evolved into wider actions about the cost of living and social security.
Elsewhere in Europe, a huge encampment of tents has occupied a square in Madrid since late last month, and thousands of people in Portugal have taken to the streets in the city of Lisbon. Tear gas and water cannons were also used on black-clad protesters in Brussels.
In Rome, many waved communist and Palestinian flags, as well as signs against the Iran war. Some let off pink smoke bombs. There was a jovial mood among the demonstrators as they lined up before the march, as has often been the case early on at previous protests, only for violence to break out later.
Protesters storm the Colosseum in Rome
Giovanna Di Matteo, a member of the left-wing Potere al Popolo! party, said she was protesting against the government that “did nothing for the people of this country.”
The government had spent money on the military “while they cut on welfare, they cut on services and people cannot reach the end of the month,” she said. “They have no money for their houses, they have no money for gasoline and everything.”
Luca, a 20-year-old medical student said the protesters felt they were “still not being heard, that everything is still the same,” and the government didn’t “care about our voice, about our voices, and about the future of this nation that is our nation.”
“We have been completely screwed by by by the fact that the wages do not keep up on on inflation and the wages in general do not keep up with the corps of living,” added Luca, asked to have his last name withheld out of fear of repercussions from law enforcement.
Major demonstrations also took place in other cities and towns across Italy.
They came after a number of protests in recent weeks have turned violent. Groups of masked protesters looted stores in Milan and elsewhere and threw projectiles at police, who responded with tear gas and water cannons earlier this month.
Italian police were out in force again Friday with riot brigades, drones and helicopters visible in the skies above the Rome protest.
Their presence was heavy after protesters stormed Rome’s historic Colosseum on Saturday, while in the south, farmers and truckers have blockaded highways and ports to protest high fuel prices which have risen since the United States and Israel launched the war against Iran.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni , who has made law and order a key tenet of her administration, said she had “great respect” for peaceful protesters on X earlier this month.
But her right-wing government has since introduced tougher penalties for rioters, including financial liability for parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.
“There is nothing revolutionary about vandalizing and stealing. Vandalism and theft are not protest, they are criminality,” Meloni said on social media after unveiling the legislation.
The government also said it would deploy 500 army troops alongside the police in Milan until the end of the year.
NBC News Chief Foreign Correspondent
Sara Monetta is a multimedia producer based in London.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia denies report that its CEO was allegedly targeted in Chinese spy plot
articles.title_zh: Nvidia denies report that its CEO was allegedly targeted in Chinese spy plot
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang reported to have had close relationship with tech company executive suspected of passing intel to China
US intelligence agencies believe the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, has been targeted by an alleged Chinese spy who had done business with him, according to a new report by the New York Times.
Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China , prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.
In the course of their surveillance, American officials determined that Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s CEO, according to the Times. Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom and have vaulted Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Donald Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
White House officials are reportedly alarmed by Alice Huang’s access to the head of Nvidia precisely because of the close relationship he has developed with Trump, according to the New York Times.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
In a statement to the New York Times, Nvidia said there was nothing out of the ordinary about the Nvidia CEO’s interactions with Alice Huang.
after newsletter promotion
“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the spokesperson said in a statement. Megaspeed and customers like it “receive ordinary business information – not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets – and zero information relevant to national security”.

articles.title_orig: Stock market today: Nasdaq dives, S&P 500 and Dow fall as Amazon, Intel earnings fuel tech rout
articles.title_zh: Stock market today: Nasdaq dives, S&P 500 and Dow fall as Amazon, Intel earnings fuel tech rout
articles.content_orig:
Intel shares plummeted 29% on Friday and headed for their worst day since 1974 after the chipmaker issued weaker-than-expected guidance due to a plant shutdown in Israel and ongoing softness in the PC market.
The stock was on pace for its second-steepest drop on record. It's a major setback for CEO Lip-Bu Tan, who was hired in March 2025, and has since been on a campaign to revive the company after it missed out on the early years of the artificial intelligence boom.
Intel's plunge is also a big hit to the Trump administration, which led the U.S. government into taking a 10% stake in the company over a year ago. While it's still a profitable investment, the value of those holdings dropped by about $12 billion on Friday. Nvidia also took a big stake in Intel, and is looking at a $6 billion drop in value.
Heading into Thursday's earnings report, Intel shares were up about 150% this year, buoyed by demand for central processors, which are becoming critical to agentic AI workloads. Analysts at D.A. Davidson downgraded the stock to neutral from buy on Friday in a report titled, "Not fixed yet."
"We understand the PC market is being impacted at the industry level," the analysts wrote. "However it is hard to justify the current multiple when weakness is so significant."
Amazon shares also sold off on Friday, slipping about 1%, after the company reported a third-quarter miss on the top and bottom line while maintaining its capital expenditure forecast for 2026 of $220 billion. Amazon also reported negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter, and a big increase from the previous period.
The Nasdaq Composite slid more than 2.5%, capping off a week of rough tech earnings. Alphabet on Thursday suffered its worst day on record, plunging more than 12%. The stock fell again on Friday.
Other semiconductor names also notched declines. Chip giant Nvidia fell 4%, while Broadcom dropped about 6% and mobile chipmaker Qualcomm tumbled 12%.
Investors are growing nervous about the massive AI spending from the tech giants and whether their investments will pay off.
"I don't think this is a moment of reckoning but I think it's a moment where investors should take a long thought about how positioning across the space still remains crowded even though the fundamentals are strong," Matt Orton, chief market strategist at Raymond James, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday.
For Intel, the disappointing forecast reflects a PC market that's getting hammered due to soaring costs for memory and other components. Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier, according to Counterpoint Research .
Intel said it expects adjusted earnings per share of 25 cents this quarter on revenue between $15 billion and $16 billion. Analysts were expecting revenue of $17.1 billion and EPS of 43 cents, according to LSEG.
"We see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," Intel finance chief David Zinsner, said in the release. "We will continue making disciplined investments in capacity and working capital to increase supply and support future growth."
The guidance also accounts for the effects of an explosion at a fab in Israel that killed two workers and seriously injured a third earlier this month. The incident will cost the company about $600 million in lost revenue over two quarters, Zinsner said.
Tan said the explosion, which he called an "unfortunate and tragic accident," caused an "extended shutdown" at the plant, impacting shipments of 10-nanometer chips.
Key to Tan's turnaround effort is Intel's foundry business, which has struggled to find its footing.
Intel is the only U.S.-based manufacturer of advanced logic chips, and is now in high-volume production of its most advanced 18A chip out of its new fab in Arizona, providing an alternative to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co . Its next Arizona fab is expected to begin operations by the end of 2028.
Intel still has no external customers for its new chips.
"We're going to have a couple of customers ready to announce the next two quarters," Tan said on the call, adding that Intel is making "tremendous progress" on its coming 14A chips.

articles.title_orig: US scraps G20 photo after European diplomats object to being pictured with Russia's Lavrov
articles.title_zh: US scraps G20 photo after European diplomats object to being pictured with Russia's Lavrov
articles.content_orig:
By WILL HALLOWELL, NEWS REPORTER and DAVID WILCOCK, DEPUTY POLITICAL EDITOR
Published: 10:57 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 12:04 EDT, 30 October 2026
A photo of diplomats from the world's 20 largest economies was reportedly scrapped after ministers refused to stand beside Russia 's Sergey Lavrov .
G20 officials, including envoys from Russia and China , are meeting in Atlanta, US, as they face deep rifts over multiple wars and other global crises that threaten international security and trade.
But plans for a group photo were axed after foreign ministers objected to being photographed with Mr Lavrov, Russia's top diplomat.
G20 participants even threatened to walk out of the summit if the photo op went ahead, according to US officials.
Already, a traditional family photo planned for Friday morning was called off shortly before the two-day meeting started.
Prior to these reports, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband had planned to boycott the 'family photo' and had asked for a separate photograph to be staged with close allies instead.
When asked on Tuesday whether he would shake hands with Mr Lavrov at the G20 summit, Mr Miliband, citing the war in Ukraine, replied: 'We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is chairing the gathering on Friday and Saturday that will set the stage for a G20 leaders ' summit hosted by Donald Trump at his Miami golf club in December.
Diplomats from the world's 20 largest economies reportedly refused to stand next to Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov (pictured) on 30 October
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, center rear, heads the opening plenary session of the G20 Foreign Ministers meeting on Friday
There appears to be little chance that the group will come to a consensus on many of the most contentious issues.
Among those are the Russia-Ukraine war, the US-Israeli war on Iran, US tariffs and Chinese machinations in the South China Sea.
All have contributed to spikes in the global cost of fuel as well as uncertainty about trade.
US officials say their top priority for the meeting is resolving differences over issues related to freedom of navigation, particularly in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, the Black Sea and the South China Sea.
The topic will include discussions on Iran, Russia-Ukraine and China and its smaller neighbors.
But hanging over the meeting is the prospect of new US military intervention in Iran, which has put the region, including G20 member Saudi Arabia, on edge.
US officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military strikes against Iran after Tuesday's midterm elections and the possibility that Iran will retaliate against them .
Some G20 countries have expressed concern that the US invited Russia, which will be represented in Atlanta by Mr Lavrov, during its heightened attacks on Ukraine.
Mr Miliband and Mr Lavrov are seated just feet apart at the G20 summit in Atlanta on Friday
China will be represented by a deputy foreign minister, but most other countries have sent their top diplomat, US officials say.
The US on Thursday scrapped plans for the family photo with G20 participants, according to two officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter.
The incident has endangered prospects for the world's largest economies to reach consensus on a number of global crises, especially the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
The US officials said Mr Rubio decided to cancel the photograph after determining that controversy over it would be a distraction.
It is unclear if Russian president Vladimir Putin will accept Mr Trump's invitation to the December summit in Florida .
US allies in Europe are uneasy with Russia's presence, especially after Mr Trump pushed ties with Ukraine to new lows by waiving fresh sanctions on Moscow and temporarily limiting logistical and intelligence assistance.
Russia's foreign ministry complained of issues securing visas for its delegation that were only resolved at the last minute.
Those complications had created the impression that 'not everyone in Washington is happy' about Mr Lavrov attending, ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
But he would use the meeting to advocate for the 'swift reform of global economic institutions' and to promote Russia's vision of a 'multipolar world', she said.
Mr Lavrov has travelled very infrequently to Nato member states since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and the resulting severe sanctions were imposed on Moscow.
His presence in Atlanta is likely to cause both domestic political problems for Mr Trump just days before the midterm elections and roil at least the G20's Western participants, according to Ian Kelly, a US ambassador to Georgia during Mr Trump's first term.
'It seems politically boneheaded to invite him,' said Mr Kelly, who now teaches international relations and diplomacy at Northwestern University outside Chicago.
Mr Kelly noted that many Republican lawmakers, who are already fearful of losing their congressional majorities, are 'cranky' with Mr Trump's conciliatory approach to Mr Putin.
Democrats, he added, could use the invitation to bash the GOP ahead of Tuesday's vote.
In terms of the G20 itself, Mr Lavrov's attendance will almost certainly hurt efforts to produce a unified approach on the Russia-Ukraine war, Mr Kelly said.
'It will definitely take away from the message that at least the Western members want to send,' he said.
Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous such meetings, was not invited this year as US officials said they made a conscious choice to only include formal members of the group.
Also missing from the Atlanta invitee list is South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group.
South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year , top US officials, including Mr Trump and Mr Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted.
South Africa said on Friday its absence from the meetings was not voluntary.
'We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,' Phindile Kunene, spokesman for South African foreign minister Ronald Lamola.
Kunene welcomed support from other G20 members that had expressed reservations about the exclusion and said South Africa was ready to participate 'on an equal footing with other members' when Britain takes over the presidency next year.
The State Department said Rubio sees the event as a way 'to advance practical cooperation on shared economic and security challenges' and his priority is for the group to seek solutions to 'geopolitical crises contributing to global economic shocks'.
It pointed to threats to freedom of navigation, energy and food security and preserving supply chains of critical minerals.
However, there is scepticism that the G20 members will be able to overcome their substantial differences.
It will be less of a meeting and more of a test, said Elaine Dezenski, the head of the Center on Economic and Financial Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington think-tank that is hawkish on Iran and other issues.
'The Atlanta meeting takes place within an environment of widening disagreement over the global economic order, and the right test is whether the US can build cooperation with partners when all member consensus appears to be out of reach,' she said during a conference call with reporters.
She said the Trump administration had shown a willingness to work – and not insignificant success – outside the G20 framework to build coalitions that advance its foreign policy goals.
'The meeting offers a chance to assess whether the US can turn shared economic security concerns into more meaningful cooperation with partners even without the consensus,' she said.

articles.title_orig: How a Democratic-controlled Congress could reshape US policy on China
articles.title_zh: How a Democratic-controlled Congress could reshape US policy on China
articles.content_orig:
A power shift would likely bring tougher scrutiny of Trump’s Beijing dealings, even as bipartisan support for a hawkish China stance endures
A Democratic takeover of either chamber of the US Congress could bring tougher scrutiny of President Donald Trump’s dealings with Beijing, even as lawmakers are likely to maintain a broadly hawkish stance towards China, analysts said.
A change in control could shift the emphasis of congressional oversight, with the Democratic Party seeking greater accountability for the administration’s China policy after Trump’s Republican Party largely gave him room to manoeuvre, said Sarah Trister, a former lead staff member on the Senate Foreign Relations subcommittee on East Asia and the Pacific.
“I would not expect congressional Democrats to come in and seek to fully reframe the China relationship,” she said.

articles.title_orig: China expels record number of officials from CCP
articles.title_zh: China expels record number of officials from CCP
articles.content_orig:
The unprecedented number of empty seats at the fifth plenum – a symbol of expulsions – serve as a symbol for the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping
China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering , which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping.
A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.
Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022. That means that more than 25% of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history.
The confirmed expulsions included Zhang Youxia, the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang. Other absences were unexplained.
“More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline,” said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, in a post on X.
The theme for this week’s plenum was party governance. Since coming to power in 2012 Xi has focused on stamping out corruption in the party. But in recent years the campaign has intensified , taking out officials in the highest ranks of the party and the military, raising questions about if the campaign is also a tool to remove political rivals or punish disloyalty.
Xi appears to have grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a lack of discipline in the ranks of the party that wields absolute authority over the state and society in China. Earlier this year he said that the party must uproot “sick trees” and that the fight against corruption was a “never-ending journey”.
A series of purges has gutted the seven-man Central Military Commission, the ruling body of China’s People’s Liberation Army. There are now just two members left: Xi himself, and the military’s anti-graft tsar, Zhang Shengmin.
Zhang was promoted to the politburo of the CCP this week, the highest ruling body in the party. Zhang is now the only military member of the senior leadership body.
The plenum also laid the groundwork for the 21st Party congress, an event which happens every five years and is expected to next be held in the second half of 2027. Xi, who is already the longest ruler of Communist China since Mao Zedong, is expected to secure a fourth term as party leader.
The ranks of the Central Committee and the politburo will be refreshed at next year’s congress, but many analysts believe that recent purges have been so wide-ranging that there are few suitable candidates to be promoted.

Frank-Walter Steinmeier was visiting Beijing at a time of heightened concern in Brussels over the widening trade gap
China and the European Union can resolve their differences through dialogue, Chinese President Xi Jinping told his German counterpart Frank-Walter Steinmeier on Friday.
“China has always regarded the European Union as a partner,” Xi said, according to state broadcaster CCTV, adding that cooperation between the two sides outweighed competition.
“As long as [both sides] stay anchored to their partnership and engage in dialogue on an equal footing, differences and challenges can always be resolved and will not stand in the way of China-EU relations moving forward,” the Chinese leader said.

articles.title_orig: Cheaper cars are selling considerably faster than at the beginning of the year
articles.title_zh: Cheaper cars are selling considerably faster than at the beginning of the year
articles.content_orig:
Consumers are concerned about rising fuel prices and affordability — and that could be showing up in how fast the least expensive cars are moving off dealer lots.
From the first quarter to the third, the number of days it took a dealer to sell a vehicle priced between $20,000 and $29,999 dropped 20%, according to data from Edmunds. That pace of selling saw the biggest acceleration of any price segment.
Vehicles priced from $30,000 to $39,999 sold about 18% faster, and the number of days it took to sell the next tier — $40,000 to $49,999 — dropped nearly 12%, according to Edmunds.
All of those price segments also took fewer days to turn than their more expensive counterparts. The lower-priced tiers took under 60 days to move off lots, with the least expensive ones selling the fastest. Every segment of vehicles above $50,000, meanwhile, took more than 60 days to sell.
"If you're a dealer and you have inventory and that price point, you're definitely noticing," said Edmunds'  Director of Insights Ivan Drury.
Cheaper vehicles may be selling faster, but they're still hard to find. The average listing price for a new vehicle in September was $49,726, according to Cox Automotive .
And, the overall sales numbers for some key segments priced under $40,000 have fallen. This has especially been true for compact cars, which are down roughly 4% since the beginning of 2026, and compact SUVs, down nearly 8% in the same period, according to Cox Automotive.
These different data points seem to be moving in opposite directions. On the one hand, cheaper cars are moving faster off dealer lots. On the other, sales of affordable segments are down.
There are a few reasons for this, according to analysts who follow the industry. One is that there might not be enough lower-priced vehicles on dealer lots in the first place.
"I think there are some supply things going on at that end of the market," said Cox Automotive Deputy Chief Economist Mark Strand. "We have to kind of grade the market on a curve  until we see what's going on with fourth-quarter data."
The compact SUV segment, in particular, is suffering from the lack of two popular models.
The Toyota RAV4 , which is the most popular SUV in the U.S., has been in short supply at many dealerships this year, as the automaker shifts production to its Kentucky factory, Strand said. The company also has shifted the entire lineup to a hybrid powertrain at a time when hybrids have been in exceptionally high demand.
The other missing SUV is the Ford Escape, which that automaker discontinued to make way for its upcoming midsize EV pickup truck.
The other slow-selling, low-priced segment — compact cars — faces structural inventory challenges, said AutoForecast Solutions Vice President of Global Forecasting Sam Fiorani.
"We've seen the disappearance of affordable, compact new vehicles over the last decade," he said.
Detroit automakers swapped out their lineups of compact coupes and sedans in favor of small crossover SUVs, which tend to carry slightly higher sticker prices than comparably sized passenger cars.
Currently, there is not a single compact passenger sedan for sale by an American manufacturer. Most on the market are Japanese or Korean, with a few German models, such as the Volkswagen Jetta and the Golf hatchback.
"You have all these brands that have just abandoned the marketplace," Fiorani said.
The smallest American passenger cars are the Ford Mustang, General Motors ' Chevrolet Corvette, and the midsize Tesla Model 3 sedan, according to AutoForecast Solutions. The firm classifies both the Mustang and the Corvette as sports cars, and as such they occupy a different niche than compact sedans like the Honda Civic or Toyota Corolla.
The Mustang has a starting price of $33,490, the Model 3 starts at $34,990, and the Chevrolet Corvette starts at $71,300. Cars like the Civic, Corolla and Jetta, meanwhile, all start below $25,000.
"Compact vehicle buyers are very price-sensitive," Fiorani said. "And so when the price of gas goes up, that eats into their car payment. That means that they can't afford a $500 or $600 a month car payment, and they have to move into the used market."
Indeed, the wholesale used prices of compact cars has risen and is up more than nearly any other segment, according to Cox Automotive. Wholesale prices — the prices vehicles sell for at large auctions, like Cox Automotive's Manheim auction — are indicators for prices overall in the fragmented used car market.
Along with the rise in prices, auto finance stats show that a historically high number of buyers are stretching to afford cars.
Roughly one in four buyers financing their purchases are getting 84-month loans — a record. Nearly three in 10 trade-ins toward new-vehicle purchases carried negative equity in the third quarter, meaning the cars being traded in were worth less than the outstanding balances of the loans on them. Shoppers are often rolling these negative balances into new loans, which pushes up the new payment cost.
Automakers have also been more tightly aligning production with demand to avoid discounting vehicles. Incentives on average are about 6.6% of the average transaction price as of October, according to Cox Automotive. Leasing offers a way to get a car with a lower payment, but leasing rates are also down.
Vehicle trade-in data suggests that many buyers who are snapping up those fast-selling cheaper vehicles are either first-time buyers or are purchasing supplemental vehicles, Edmunds' Drury said.
The subcompact SUV segment is one lower-priced group that has seen sales rise in 2026. That is a segment that attracts a lot of first-time buyers. But this is still a relatively small share of the total car market, Fiorani said.
"It's not the mainstream vehicle that Americans want," he said. "It is the vehicle that entry-level buyers need to get to work, to get to school. ... It's people who don't have families yet."
Repeat buyers are less likely to want to step down into a compact car or SUV, Drury said.
"The moment you get into that other vehicle and it's a little bit smaller, it's not as comfortable, it doesn't fit all your stuff, all your kid's equipment for soccer practice, you're done," he said. "You're not giving up 360 cameras, ventilated seats, heated steering wheels, these niceties that you've become accustomed to.  Automakers know that too. Dealers know that."
The truly cash-strapped are either snapping up the relatively few low-priced cars on dealer lots, moving to the used market, or holding on to their cars longer.
"The people who are trying to buy the smaller vehicles are really hurt by the way the economy is at the moment," Fiorani said. "So those people are trying to move into used vehicles or trying to maintain their current vehicle as long as they can. Automakers should be prepared for a softening in the marketplace."

articles.title_orig: Democratic senator blames Egypt press crackdown on Trump military aid decision
articles.title_zh: Democratic senator blames Egypt press crackdown on Trump military aid decision
articles.content_orig:
A top Democratic senator has blamed a crackdown on independent journalism in Egypt on a decision by the Trump administration to waive human rights conditions on US military funding to the country.
Chris Murphy, who sits on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, accused the US government of "abandoning" the Egyptian people after it lifted restrictions relating to more than $300m of defence assistance.
Over the last month a series of arrests has taken place of journalists at two of the few remaining independent news outlets in Egypt, where newspapers and TV stations are closely controlled by the authorities.
The US State Department told the BBC it waived conditions on a portion of military aid to Egypt in September due to the country's "importance to US national security interests".
Murphy, speaking at the Middle East Institute (MEI) in Washington this week, said he was in no doubt the two were linked.
"The minute that money was released, the crackdown began in an absolutely devastating way," he said.
On Tuesday a court in Cairo ordered the closure of the news website Madr Masa and fined its editor-in-chief Lina Attalah in what Amnesty International called "a crushing blow to press freedom".
Earlier this month, authorities arrested six journalists at the independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh and charged them with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
The Egyptian Embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment.
Cairo has remained a close regional ally of the US despite what human rights groups say are widespread abuses under President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's government, including torture and enforced disappearances.
Sisi denies there are political prisoners in Egypt. He has previously said stability and security are paramount, adding authorities have promoted rights by trying to provide basic needs such as jobs and housing.
Washington sends Egypt £1.3bn ($1.73bn) per year, making it one of the world's biggest recipients of US military assistance.
US law allows up to £320m of the funding to be withheld, conditioned on Egypt meeting democracy and human rights requirements. But these restrictions can be waived by the administration on national security grounds.
In September, Secretary of State Marco Rubio waived human rights conditions on $320m of military aid in light of Egypt's role since the launch of the US war with Iran, according to a letter addressed to various Congressional committees. Egypt assisted negotiations between the US and Iran.
Exercising the waiver authority was "essential" for the US-Egypt relationship, "particularly in light of Egypt's helpful role following Operation Epic Fury," according to the September 4 memo seen by Reuters which bore Rubio's signature.
Asked by the BBC about the move in light of this month's arrests of journalists, the State Department said the waiver was "due to Egypt's importance to US national security interests, the concrete security cooperation Egypt provides to the United States, and the need to maintain that cooperation to address regional security challenges".
It added it maintained dialogue with Cairo on a "full range of issues" but would "not comment on private diplomatic conversations".
Rubio's move followed a similar decision by the Biden administration in 2024, when then Secretary of State Anthony Blinken waived human rights conditions to grant the full military aid allocation to Egypt as the US sought Cairo's role in mediating between Israel and Hamas in the war in Gaza.
Under Biden prior to 2024, the US withheld portions of the annual military allocation over Egypt's human rights record.
Murphy, who chairs a congressional committee on the Middle East and counterterrorism, said he had been a critic of both the Biden and Trump administrations over the issue.
"To the extent that there was any glimmer left of political speech in Egypt, it is gone for one proximate reason: The United States government abandoned the people of Egypt and decided to remove all conditions on our funding," Murphy told the MEI.
"Any hope of a true, meaningful political opposition rebirthing in Egypt has been shattered by this decision," he added.
US military aid to Cairo began after the 1978 Camp David Accords and the peace treaty that followed between Egypt and Israel. Successive administrations have viewed the world's most populous Arab country as a critical US ally in the region.
The group Reporters Without Borders describes Egypt as one of the world's biggest jailers of journalists.
The conviction of Lina Attalah and the closure of Madr Masr marked an unprecedented escalation in repression of press freedoms in Egypt, according to Timothy E Kaldas, Deputy Director of The Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, a Washington DC-based think tank.
He said both the US and European Union had been prioritising their strategic relations with Egypt over human rights and the rule of law in the country.
"It's been fostering a sense of impunity on the part of the Egyptian authorities that we're seeing play out," he told the BBC.
"Egypt is getting signals from both sides of the Atlantic that human rights and the rule of law are no longer a priority, and they're testing the limits of that."
He added: "The fact that they're not getting more robust pushback reinforces the wrong message."

articles.title_orig: Three tankers strike mines and catch fire in Strait of Hormuz, Iran claims, and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Three tankers strike mines and catch fire in Strait of Hormuz, Iran claims, and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
Iran said four tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz and Yemen's Houthis claimed missile strikes on Saudi Arabia, escalating pressure on two fronts as the U.S. reportedly weighs renewed military action against Tehran after Tuesday's midterm elections.
The flare-up is fueling concern among regional officials and analysts that fighting could resume around the Nov. 3 vote, even as Vice President JD Vance seeks to reopen talks with Iran.
The developments underscore the competing diplomatic and military tracks now shaping the conflict, which now in its ninth month.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said three tankers caught fire after striking mines along what it called an "unauthorized southern route" near the Omani coast. Iran's army said a fourth burned east of the strait.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported a small boat attaching two explosive devices to a tanker about 25 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman. The blasts sparked an engine-room fire that disabled the vessel, the agency said, adding that the crew was safe.
Separately, Iran's Revolutionary Guards on Thursday also challenged a U.S. Central Command statement that American forces had cleared mines from the primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz. The vital waterway carried about one-fifth of the world's energy supplies, and has seen traffic plummet to single-digit daily passings since the war started in late February.
"Prove the claim that the Strait of Hormuz has been cleared of mines with independent evidence, not a statement," IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebi said. "The reality of the Strait of Hormuz is determined in the air, on land and at sea, not on social media and in America's media war rooms."
Iran-backed Houthi forces said they launched six military operations across Saudi Arabia, targeting airports and oil facilities, despite a rare meeting of Saudi and Iranian senior officials in Tehran earlier this week. The two sides had agreed to resolve regional differences through dialogue.
Saudi authorities have not confirmed the attacks but said their air defenses have intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone launched toward the holy Mecca region.
Earlier this week, Vance sent a letter via Qatari mediators to Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, proposing a framework for talks.
President Donald Trump, when asked whether he directed the outreach, said "no," framing it as Iran needing " help with medical supplies and various things ." "He [Vance] asked me what I thought. I said, 'if you want to do that, that's OK,'" Trump said.
Reports have emerged that the Trump administration may resume military actions in the Middle East after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Adm. Brad Cooper, top U.S. commander in the region briefed Trump on military options for Iran in a rare in-person visit to the White House, the Wall Street Journal reported late Thursday, citing unnamed U.S. officials close to the matter.
The meeting, joined by other cabinet members, covered other topics including the continuing U.S. blockade, according to the report.

articles.title_orig: Spanish minister refuses to resign over second major train crash on his watch
articles.title_zh: Spanish minister refuses to resign over second major train crash on his watch
articles.content_orig:
This blog is now closed, you can read more on this story here
Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has admitted “trust in high-speed rail has been broken” after Wednesday’s deadly train collision that killed at least 69 people, injured more than 100 and prompted a national debate on the safety of the country’s rail network.
Sánchez said the Spanish state was “working tirelessly” to provide information as quickly as possible to the families of the victims – who include people from at least 23 different foreign countries – adding that his government was committed to finding what had caused Spain’s second deadly train collision this year.
Two trains, one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo, were travelling from Madrid towards the southern region of Andalucía on Wednesday when they collided just before 9am . After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other slammed into its rear , knocking several carriages off the track near Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha.
The crash came nine months after 46 people were killed and dozens injured when two trains – one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.
“ It’s unacceptable for a country like Spain – which has such a powerful high-speed rail system – to experience two accidents of this nature and magnitude within a single year,” the prime minister said on Friday.
“Therefore, our task isn’t merely to investigate the causes of what occurred, but also to provide solutions to further strengthen our nation’s high-speed rail system.
Public trust in the high-speed system has been broken ; the government’s responsibility goes beyond diagnosing the causes – it must also offer solutions to ensure that a tragedy of this scale doesn’t happen again.”
Shortly after Sánchez spoke, Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente – who is under growing pressure to resign – gave a press conference in which he dismissed calls to step down, promising instead to focus on “providing the Spanish people with solutions” to restore trust.
“My duty now isn’t to talk about whether or not I carry on with my job; it’s to solve the problems, clarify what happened and offer clear explanations,” he said. “ The most important thing I can do is offer solutions as best I can. If the investigation shows there were failures of organisation or control, we will act accordingly. And if individuals are found to be responsible, action will be taken.”
Puente once again suggested that responsibility for Wednesday’s crash appeared to lie within the Madrid control centre of Spain’s state infrastructure operator, Adif. He said that in the run-up to the crash, the LZB signalling system – which automatically halts a train if the line ahead is occupied – had gone down, but stressed that such incidents were not at all uncommon. Once the system was down, he said, control and decision-making powers ultimately reverted to humans, as was the case in other transport sectors.
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today .

Bulgaria’s next president will be elected in a runoff vote on Sunday, after a close race between the two main contenders ended inconclusively in the first round.
The incumbent Iliana Yotova , former vice-president to Bulgaria’s former president and current prime minister Rumen Radev , faces pro-European opposition candidate, Andrey Gyurov.
The two candidates will pit contrasting political visions against each other in a highly polarised contest on Sunday, AP noted.
Contrary to pre-election expectations by observers for a double-digit difference in favour of Yotova, her opponent showed a surprisingly strong performance coming just 2.8 percentage points behind her and leaving all options open for the runoff.
AP noted that Bulgarians vote against a backdrop of growing economic hardship and drone attacks on Black Sea shipping, which have left several sailors dead or missing.
Polls will open 7am local time and close 8pm local time.
The Russian independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta has announced it is closing, citing pressure from authorities who recently searched the home of its senior editor and earlier this year detained one of its journalists.
“Novaya Gazeta is ceasing to exist,” the editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, said in a video statement published on YouTube on Friday. “The Russian authorities – the Russian special services – have forced the editorial team to end its work.”
Russia has introduced near-Soviet levels of censorship since sending troops to Ukraine, pushing the vast majority of independent journalists into exile. Novaya Gazeta, a bastion of independent journalism in Russia, is classed by Moscow as a “foreign agent”, a label used to stifle dissent.
Sokolov said: “ Novaya Gazeta has been killed … On 9 November we will turn off the lights in our home, where we have lived for 30 years. We will shut down the servers and leave.”
This month Sokolov was taken in for questioning and Russian authorities searched his home over a criminal case involving one of his colleagues, Oleg Roldugin, who was arrested in April.
Russia has intensified its crackdown on independent news outlets since its offensive on Ukraine in February 2022. Novaya Gazeta cut down production inside Russia after the offensive began. Authorities revoked its media licence the same year.
The paper’s then editor-in-chief, Dmitry Muratov, jointly won the Nobel peace prize in 2021 for his “efforts to safeguard freedom of expression” at the helm of the paper.
In Belgrade’s Pioneers Park, just across from the national assembly, a small crowd craned their necks to listen. One woman held aloft a placard reading “Love prevailed for the people and Serbia”.
With a bouquet of media microphones in front of them, members of the Student List, the direct democracy movement that won an improbable but decisive victory in Sunday’s election, gathered under the trees.
Student List candidate Svetlana Stanarević was applauded when she accused the officials of violating the law. She also called for the director of Serbia’s internal intelligence agency to resign, accusing him of running the organisation as “a party security service, not a state security service”.

articles.title_orig: Celebrate Warhammer Day with some suitably scary miniatures
articles.title_zh: Celebrate Warhammer Day with some suitably scary miniatures
articles.content_orig:
Celebrate Warhammer Day with some suitably scary miniatures
Saturday is Warhammer Day ! It’s also Halloween, so, to get ready we’re taking a look at some of our favourite terrifying Warhammer miniatures.
Their whispered war cry is the last thing you’ll hear. These living suits of armour can’t be reasoned with, can’t be stopped, and they’re armed with magic guns!
Once proud Space Marines, Rubric Marines are now nothing more than a pile of dust and a corrupted soul, trapped inside a suit of power armour for all time, and commanded like a puppet by the arcane magic of warp-fuelled sorcerers. Some fates are worse than death.
What would Halloween be without vampires? Blood Angels may not dislike garlic, but they are incredibly stylish, and do crave the taste of blood. Just remember, Space Marines have two hearts, so you’d better bring two stakes!
Blood Angels have a second flaw – the Black Rage – and none have ever truly been able to overcome it. That was until Mephiston , Chief Librarian of the Blood Angels, crossed the Rubicon Primaris and seemingly left his curse behind him. Don’t think he won’t nibble your neck though.
While they may look skeletal, there’s no organic matter to be found on a Necron Warrior . These deathless automatons march without fear or mercy in eerie lockstep with a single-minded desire to destroy every living creature in the galaxy. You may be faster, but they’ll chase you forever.
Necron Warriors form the undead legions of the dynasties, and if it wasn’t scary enough staring into their dead, soulless eyes, then their guns can flay the flesh from any living creature. On top of that, one of their star gods was death incarnate, and is said to be the inspiration for the grim reaper .
The Nighthaunt are no mere ghosts, they are bitter, ethereal spirits that inflict terror, and drag down the souls of the living. Not to put too fine a point on it, these are not kids wearing bedsheets with eyeholes cut into them.
No figure in the worlds of Warhammer embodies the misery of the restless undead more than Lady Olynder, Mortarch of Grief . She is despair made manifest, gloom given form, and mortals in her presence are overwhelmed by a dread so potent that it can silence the heartbeat of even the strongest opponent.
While the motley assortment of creatures that make up the Gloomspite Gitz may seem “fun” to the casual observer, make no mistake, Squigs have very sharp teeth. And a lot of them.
When grots take to the battlefield with a horde of Squigs , woe betide anyone who underestimates these vicious creatures. Little more than mouths with legs and a terrible appetite, Squigs are feared across the Mortal Realms, able to tear even the mightiest foe to shreds in a crimson blur.
The full moon shines down through the inky black darkness. Out on the moor, you hear a blood-curdling howl. Wulfen are part Space Marine and part wolf, and they are probably the closest thing to a werewolf in the 41st Millennium.
Wulfen are bestial warriors, altered by the curse lying in the gene-seed of all scions of the Wolf King – hunters that bound forward with fangs bared and claws outstretched. They’re fast, and they hit hard with claws, teeth, and a variety of deadly weapons.
Join us in-store to celebrate Warhammer Day and Halloween! You’ll be able to pick up other scary models, such as skeletons , zombies , and other undead warriors . Plus, you can get Oath Fulfilled , the special commemorative miniature, who, if she gets sufficiently blessed by the Dark Gods, might make it onto this list for next year.

articles.title_orig: Putin open to phone call with Zelensky, Ukraine suspects a Kremlin trap
articles.title_zh: Putin open to phone call with Zelensky, Ukraine suspects a Kremlin trap
articles.content_orig:
The Kremlin is seeking to avoid a face-to-face meeting between President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin by proposing they speak by phone instead, the Kyiv Independent has learned.
The apparent move comes as Kyiv insists the two leaders should meet in person to address the most pressing issues in negotiations , including Russia's territorial demands and security guarantees. Such a meeting would be their first since 2019.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Oct. 30 that Putin was "open to dialogue with everyone." Asked whether the Russian leader would speak with Zelensky by phone, Peskov added that "no one has called yet."
The comments came as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the U.S. in Abu Dhabi, which Kyiv sees as a possible starting point for a meeting between the countries' leaders.
Ukrainian officials privately suspect Moscow is trying to arrange a phone call that they believe would achieve little while avoiding the prospect of a face-to-face meeting.
"They've already tried to do this over the phone," one senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.
Kyiv has long pushed for a direct meeting between Zelensky and Putin.
The two leaders last met in person in Paris in December 2019 during the Normandy Format talks mediated by France and Germany. They have not held direct talks since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Ukraine has made several attempts to arrange a meeting since then.
Zelensky invited Putin to Istanbul for talks on May 16, 2025, proposing a trilateral meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump to advance peace efforts. Putin declined to attend and instead sent a delegation led by a low-level presidential aide, Vladimir Medinsky.
After meeting Putin in Alaska in August 2025, the U.S. president said he was working to arrange a meeting between the Russian and Ukrainian leaders.
Trump later said Putin was reluctant to meet Zelensky because "he doesn't like him."
Now, every time the Ukrainian side raises the idea of a meeting at the level of leaders, the Kremlin challenges the Ukrainian president to come to Moscow for it. Zelensky has called for Putin to meet him in a neutral location.
Kyiv continues to argue that only direct talks between the leaders can produce meaningful decisions on the most difficult issues. Ukrainian officials say the Russian representatives sent to negotiations do not have the authority to make such decisions.
"Territorial issues can only be discussed by the leaders of the countries at war, and only at their level," Zelensky told reporters on Oct. 27. "No one else has the authority to do so."
Territory remains one of the main obstacles to an agreement.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected a ceasefire and demanded that Kyiv surrender the parts of Ukrainian Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts that Russian forces have failed to capture. The strategically important regions in eastern Ukraine remain central to the negotiations.
Ukraine, by contrast, has called for a ceasefire along the current front line.
Several people familiar with the matter told the Kyiv Independent that Washington supports the idea of a leaders' meeting and that Trump could help arrange one.
The G20 summit in Miami in December could serve as a possible venue, the people said. Under this scenario, if Putin accepts Trump's invitation to attend, Zelensky could also travel there to meet the Russian leader.
As Ukraine pushes for a meeting, its officials believe Moscow is trying to undermine the effort by offering alternatives that would not require Putin to meet Zelensky.
One senior Ukrainian official questioned whether a phone call could resolve the issues at stake without U.S. involvement.
"Well, what do we want? To reach a final decision on key issues and security guarantees ," the official told the Kyiv Independent. "Is it possible to do this over the phone — and only over the phone — without the U.S.? No."
"We need a trilateral format with the U.S., plus some involvement from the Europeans ... But they're like, 'Well, just go to Moscow ,' or call us, but what good will a phone call do?"
Ukrainian officials fear that Moscow's insistence on a phone call could give it another reason to walk away from negotiations without making meaningful commitments. They argue a meeting with third parties would better address the disputes.
Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S. plan to hold talks in Abu Dhabi in November, focusing on steps to de-escalate the war. Moscow has signaled readiness to resume negotiations with Kyiv after a pause of more than eight months.
Zelensky said the planned technical talks should seek concrete progress on de-escalation, including an energy and maritime ceasefire, prisoner exchanges , and discussions about a possible trilateral meeting between the leaders.
"We hope for a result regarding energy and at sea, an exchange of prisoners, and a discussion of the possible format for a trilateral meeting at the leaders' level."
Kyiv does not expect working-level negotiations alone to end the war.
Ukrainian officials say Putin must take part in the process himself if the talks are to produce actual decisions.
"Putin needs to come out of his bunker and take part in the trilateral talks," the senior Ukrainian official said. "And personally confirm that he is ending the war."
Tim Zadorozhnyy is a reporter at the Kyiv Independent covering foreign policy, U.S.-Ukraine relations, and political developments across Europe and Russia. He studied International Relations and European Studies at Lazarski University and Coventry University. Tim began his journalism career in Odesa in 2022 as a reporter for a local television channel. He later spent a year and a half at the Belarusian independent media outlet NEXTA, first as a news anchor and later as a managing editor. He is fluent in English, Ukrainian, and Russian.

articles.title_orig: What next as Netanyahu's party claims Israel's election was stolen?
articles.title_zh: What next as Netanyahu's party claims Israel's election was stolen?
articles.content_orig:
Tel Aviv — Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party alleged Thursday that Israel's election earlier in the week was stolen by Arab-majority parties, helped by foreign funding that amounted to vote-buying, as final results showed Netanyahu's bloc has lost its majority in Israel's parliament, the Knesset.
Israel's Arab-majority parties had their highest turnout ever in Tuesday's election, winning an unprecedented 19 of the Knesset's 120 seats. Their success is one of the main reasons Netanyahu's bloc lost its majority and can't now form a new government.
The final election results show the far-right wing bloc's share of Knesset seats fell from 68 to 53.
Israel's Arab minority, also called Palestinian citizens of Israel, makes up about 20% of the country's population.
"Israel's elections have been stolen," Netanyahu's Likud party declared in a statement Thursday, claiming "an attack on democracy aimed at leading to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel, and the overthrow of the right-wing government to cause a withdrawal and defeat of the IDF (Israeli military) on all fronts — first and foremost, Iran."
The four parties that make up the main bloc opposing Netanyahu won 48 seats, so they would need some support from the Arab parties to try to form a coalition government, assuming none of the lawmakers currently aligned with Netanyahu's bloc defect.
The heads of Israel's two biggest Arab parties, which collectively won 19 seats, have said they would be willing to help the main opposition bloc oust Netanyahu from power.
Most of the Jewish-led parties that oppose Netanyahu vowed before the election not to rely on support from Arab parties to form a government, however, leaving a question mark over whether they might now be willing to cooperate to build a coalition to unseat the incumbent prime minister.
The Shin Bet, Israel's internal security agency, said it had opened an investigation into possible foreign influence in the election, but the scope of that investigation has not been made clear.
"An investigation of this type is also focused and bounded, and does not cast aspersions or place blame on an entire sector that went out to vote democratically and legally," the agency said in a Thursday statement.
The Acting Director-General of the Central Elections Committee, Din Livne, said in a letter to a committee member on Thursday that "there is no basis to the claims regarding a systematic compromise of the integrity of the elections."
Israel media reports said one of the allegations the Shin Bet investigation would consider was whether Qatar had sent money to Arab parties in order to increase turnout among Arab Israeli voters.
Qatar's foreign ministry has denied the accusation.
"We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome," ministry spokesperson Majid Al-Ansari said. "Qatar should not be used as a scapegoat for the political failures of certain Israeli politicians."
While vote counting is now officially complete, the election results must still be certified and sent to President Issac Herzog before a new parliament can be sworn in and the process of forming a new government begins.
Gadi Eisenkot, head of the centrist Yashar party and the top candidate to replace Netanyahu as prime minister, said he was worried that Netanyahu could be using the allegation of a stolen election to justify delaying or disqualifying the results.
"Netanyahu, who has accustomed himself to dealing with reality through lies, consciousness engineering, and the spreading of chaos, is leading alongside his partners an improper influence operation on the Israeli public aimed at delaying the publication of the election results on time and creating fictitious delegitimization of the activity of the 26th Knesset," Eisenkot said Thursday in a social media post.
Once the new Knesset is sworn in — even without a new government decided on —   Eisenkot's bloc, along with the Arab parties, could begin passing laws given that they will control a majority in the parliament.
Netanyahu, who President Trump endorsed enthusiastically , will remain in his post as a caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed. If the parties cannot negotiate to form a new coalition government, then the country would have to hold the election all over again, and Netanyahu would remain the prime minister in the interim.

articles.title_orig: Treasury Department announces new Series I bond rate of 5.51% for the next six months
articles.title_zh: Treasury Department announces new Series I bond rate of 5.51% for the next six months
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Department of the Treasury has announced new rates for Series I bonds.
Newly purchased I bonds will pay 5.51% annual interest from Nov. 1 through April 30, which is up from the 4.26% yield offered on purchases made through Oct. 31.
The new rate includes a variable portion of 4.08% based on inflation data , and a fixed portion of 1.40%. The fixed rate is up from 0.90% announced in April, and the highest since 2006.
Combined, the composite I bond rate is 5.51% after rounding, according to the Treasury.
Amid the post-pandemic inflation peak , the I bond rate hit a record high of 9.62% in May 2022, and investors poured millions into the government-backed, nearly risk-free asset.
As inflation cooled and I bond rates fell, many short-term investors redeemed I bonds . But investors could return as inflation pushes I bond rates back up, experts say.
"I bonds are a lot more attractive at this point," said David Enna, founder of Tipswatch.com, a website that tracks Treasury inflation-protected securities, or TIPS, and I bond rates .
The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September 2026 from one year earlier, up from an annual pace of 3.4% in August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported in October.
In September, some higher inflation came from the Iran war, which pushed up gasoline and energy costs . President Donald Trump 's tariffs, new artificial intelligence data centers and demand for travel have also added to rising prices , economists say.
Consumers expect rising inflation to continue. In September, the one-year inflation outlook jumped to 3.9%, the highest in more than three years, according to a New York Fed survey released in early October.
I bond rates have a variable and fixed rate portion , which the Treasury adjusts every six months, in May and November.
The variable rate is tied to inflation — using the consumer price index percentage change over six months — and stays the same for six months after you purchase, regardless of the Treasury's next update.
Your fixed rate doesn't change after purchasing I bonds. The Treasury doesn't disclose how it calculates fixed-rate adjustments, making it harder to predict.
Some experts believe the I bond fixed rate could be driven by real, or inflation-adjusted, yields from five-year TIPS, according to Ken Tumin, founder of DepositQuest.com, a blog that tracks I bond rates, among other deposit accounts.
"There's some uncertainty there," Tumin said.
If you currently own I bonds, rate updates follow a six-month timeline based on your original purchase date.
After you own I bonds for six months, the variable yield changes to the next announced rate. But the fixed rate stays the same for the entire time you own the asset.
For example, let's say you purchased I bonds in March when the variable rate was still 3.12% and the fixed rate was 0.9%. After six months, the variable portion would shift to 3.34%, announced in April 2026 , but your fixed rate would remain 0.9%.
You can earn I bond interest for up to 30 years, or less if you redeem the assets before that. However, you can't cash in I bonds for at least one year after you buy them. If you redeem within five years, you lose your last three months of interest.

articles.title_orig: ExxonMobil and Chevron report blowout profits as Trump touts benefits of high oil prices
articles.title_zh: ExxonMobil and Chevron report blowout profits as Trump touts benefits of high oil prices
articles.content_orig:
It’s a good time to be an oil company.
The two largest U.S. oil companies, ExxonMobil and Chevron, on Friday reported blowout profits that easily beat expectations as oil prices remain sharply elevated because of the U.S. war with Iran.
ExxonMobil reported a profit that doubled from the same period last year, while Chevron’s earnings surged more than 180% from a year earlier.
As part of the bumper returns, Exxon said it was increasing the dividend it pays to investors.
The returns at both companies came as the price of oil surged beyond $100 per barrel and has remained there for months. On Friday, prices accelerated again, with Brent oil trading just under $118 per barrel.
The highest level that Brent reached since the United States and Israel launched the Iran war in late February was $126, which it is now approaching again.
Since the start of the year, Exxon shares have risen 52%, and Chevron shares have returned 50%.
Overnight, another major oil company, BP, reported that its profit skyrocketed to an 18-year high.
The average price of regular gasoline has soared 40% for consumers since the war broke out. Soaring prices continue to pressure consumers ahead of the midterm elections, where voters have repeatedly said that prices and inflation are primary concerns.
In 2024, Donald Trump repeatedly pledged to drive energy costs down . “My plan will cut energy prices in half or more than that within 12 months of taking office,” the then-candidate said in September 2024, while adding that it would mean “gasoline below $2 a gallon.”
As of Friday, the average gasoline price is currently more than double that.
In recent rallies on the campaign trail, the president has celebrated the higher oil and gas profits. “I wonder if I should say this,” Trump mused aloud during a rally Oct. 24, before saying “our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what’s happened in the Middle East.”
Trump touts U.S. oil business making ‘hundreds of billions’
“My people said, ‘Please don’t mention that, sir,’ because people are paying a little higher,” Trump continued. “But what we’ve done for this country, we’re making money like this country has never made before.”
“I don’t give a damn: I’m going to say it. We’re making a freaking fortune.”
The higher prices are also a result of the war between Ukraine and Russia following President Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of his neighbor in 2022.
“There’s a lot of disruption happening in the world,” ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods told CNBC on Friday morning . “What you’re finding is because of the closure” in the Strait of Hormuz, “shipping has to find new routes around to continue to deliver the products that society desperately needs.”
“About half of Russia’s refinery capacity has been taken out from the Ukraine bombing,” he added.
“That shortage of refining capacity and availability to the world is what’s driving product prices as high as it is, and frankly, diesel is the key crunch point here because it is so critical to economic growth,” Woods continued.
Since the start of the year, the average nationwide price for diesel fuel has risen 78%. New York-traded diesel futures have soared 130% since the start of the year, likely indicating more price rises could still come at the pump.
Both Exxon and Chevron said that they were running their refineries at maximum output to continue making as much diesel as possible.
Trump has taken specific note of the impact that diesel could have on the economy. The administration has quickly issued multiple orders and policies in an attempt to bring prices down.
The president signed an order allowing more widespread use of an off-road dyed variety of diesel, has pressured European allies to release more of the diesel reserves into the global market, and has announced a deal with Putin for some of that country’s diesel supplies.
Trump’s latest move came last week, when he announced $150 million in Defense Production Act funding to “expand petroleum production, storage, and logistics at refineries across.”
The moves have not meaningfully brought prices down.
On Friday, Woods said his refineries were already being pushed to the limit. “We are at record levels of utilization for our refineries,” he said on CNBC.
“If you look at North America, we produce record volumes of diesel. That’s all been a function of trying to drive more product into the marketplace to meet that demand and to drive costs down.”
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: iOS 27.2 adds new Find My feature at just the right time
articles.title_zh: iOS 27.2 adds new Find My feature at just the right time
articles.content_orig:
iOS 27.2 is here, and alongside new features for Apple Photos , Messages , and Siri AI , the update also has a welcome addition for Find My: support for Apple TV 4K remotes.
Find My has long been the iPhone’s go-to hub for locating people as well as your Apple devices.
Except until now, there’s been one Apple device not included in the app.
The Siri Remote for Apple TV 4K has historically been absent from Find My. There was another way to locate it using the Remote app via Control Center, but most users probably didn’t realize that feature existed.
But with iOS 27.2, Apple TV remotes have now been added to the Find My app for location tracking. Open Find My in iOS 27.2 and go to the Devices tab, and compatible Siri Remotes (2nd gen and later) will now appear there.
It’s nice that Apple finally addressed this oversight, but the timing is no coincidence. That’s because the new Siri Remote (4th gen) is going to make finding a lost remote way easier.
The new remote features Precision Finding support and a built-in speaker . So the next time it’s lost somewhere in your house, your iPhone can direct you step-by-step to its location and trigger a noise to help.
The new Siri Remote is included with the 4th generation Apple TV 4K. But you can also buy it separately for $59 and get the same new features.
The upgraded remote is compatible with all Apple TV 4K and Apple TV HD models. To benefit from Precision Finding though, you’ll need an iPhone 17 or newer.
Did you know the Remote app offered support for finding a lost remote? Will you use the new feature in Find My? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: Binance Hack Sends Crypto Stocks Tumbling
articles.title_zh: Binance Hack Sends Crypto Stocks Tumbling
articles.content_orig:
Coinbase Global earned third-quarter adjusted net income of $719 million , up 66% from $433 million a year ago, largely due to a recovery in the cryptocurrency market.
Coinbase said it earned $2.51 a share in the latest quarter, although it wasn't immediately clear if that compared with the 6-cent-per-share profit that Wall Street analysts had estimated. Revenue of $1.20 billion trailed the $1.233 billion expected by analysts polled by LSEG.
Net income at the San Francisco-based platform surged thanks to the value of its volatile cryptocurrency investment portfolio, which can swing wildly even when the composition of the underlying holdings are little changed.
The third quarter value of Coinbase's crypto investment portfolio climbed due to a resurgence in the digital asset market. The price of bitcoin — often used as a gauge for all crypto assets — rose 39% in the three-month period ended Sept. 30 and the flagship cryptocurrency recently changed hands at roughly $80,809.
In the third quarter, Coinbase deepened its push into non-crypto products and services, including artificial intelligence integrations for traders, tokenized real-world assets and prediction markets.
In July, VP of product Max Branzburg told CNBC that Coinbase would debut an "everything exchange" spotlighting tokenized stocks and other real-world assets, derivatives trading, prediction markets and early-stage token sales. The trading platform also introduced Coinbase for Agents in early October, supporting users that want to use ChatGPT, Muse or other AI agents to manage their portfolios or research and trade various assets.
Coinbase also expanded its prediction market offerings, making a wider range of event contracts available to users.
In the third quarter, prediction markets revenue grew to more than $200 million on an annual basis, while the number of traders on those markets increased 60% compared with the second quarter.

articles.title_orig: This electric screwdriver uses a camera and AI to figure out what bit you need
articles.title_zh: This electric screwdriver uses a camera and AI to figure out what bit you need
articles.content_orig:
The Arrowspace S1 can identify the bit and then show you where to find it in an optional smart case.
The Arrowspace S1 can identify the bit and then show you where to find it in an optional smart case.
Companies like Hoto and Fanttik have elevated the design and functionality of tools like electric screwdrivers , but Arrowmax wants to make them smarter by adding a camera and AI that work together to eliminate the trial and error of finding the exact type and size of bit you need. It’s convenient, but also helpful, as choosing the wrong size could potentially leave you with a stripped screw and a much harder repair.
Arrowmax is making the Arrowspace S1 available through a Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign , but the company has already successfully crowdfunded other products. You can preorder the screwdriver by itself for around $79, but its functionality and usefulness is expanded by bundling it with the S1 smart bit case that bumps the preorder price to around $129. Full retail pricing will be higher, and the S1 isn’t expected to ship until April 2027 at the earliest.
On the bottom of the S1 is a small camera with an LED light that’s used to capture an image of a screw head. To ensure the screwdriver’s AI model has the best possible image to work with, next to the camera is a “precision contact probe” that extends and rests on the surface of the screw to ensure the camera is always at the ideal focus distance.
Once the AI processes the photo, the type and size of bit you need will be displayed through a connected mobile app. Based on the identified screw, the screwdriver will also automatically select a safe torque setting to reduce the risk of damaging the fastener. To save you the trouble of having to find the exact bit that’s needed, the optional S1 Smart Case has a collection of 52 steel bits with an LED next to each one that lights up so the one you need is easy to spot.
The Arrowspace S1 features a 600mAh rechargeable battery the company claims delivers enough power to run for up to 90 minutes, or tighten or loosen over 900 screws. That performance will vary if you turn off the automatic torque adjustments and increase it yourself. The remaining charge is displayed on the screwdriver’s OLED screen which also shows the current torque setting and which direction it’s set to rotate.

articles.title_orig: iPadOS 27.2: Two new features just upgraded your iPad
articles.title_zh: iPadOS 27.2: Two new features just upgraded your iPad
articles.content_orig:
iPadOS 27.2 arrived this week as the latest noteworthy iPad software update, here are two new features it includes.
Siri AI is a major improvement over the old Siri, and I’m using it all the time on my iPad—often with a CMD + Space keyboard shortcut since Siri and Spotlight are now integrated.
In iPadOS 27.2, Apple added another convenient way to interact with Siri that first debuted on the Mac in macOS Golden Gate.
When you select text in iPadOS 27.2 via a trackpad or mouse, there’s a new Siri contextual popup that appears to the left of your selection. If you hover over the Siri icon with your cursor, it instantly expands to offer an ‘Ask Siri’ text field.
This makes it quick and easy to ask Siri about whatever you’ve highlighted. And if you’re in the writing process, the Siri popup even has suggestions like ‘Proofread,’ ‘Rewrite,’ and ‘How does this sound?’ so you can get help with just a click.
Siri AI also includes several new upgrades that make it more capable. Per Apple’s release notes :
iPads make great video devices whether you’re an adult or a kid. And if you share an iPad with a partner or child, the Apple TV app has a welcome new addition: user profiles.
iPadOS 27.2 brings over the same profiles feature that tvOS already offered on Apple TV 4K.
When you open the Apple TV app on iPad, you’ll see a new profile selection screen at startup. From here, you can choose who’s watching and the TV app will automatically update its queue, playback history, and content recommendations based on your selection.
If you’re a parent, profiles will take content restrictions into account. So when your child’s profile is active, they’ll only see films and TV shows that match the age settings you’ve previously set.
And if you don’t want to use profiles, it’s easy to disable them from showing on startup with a quick tap.

articles.title_orig: Canadian family desperately 'tried to fight off' masked intruders before CEO and daughters shot, wife attacked
articles.title_zh: Canadian family desperately 'tried to fight off' masked intruders before CEO and daughters shot, wife attacked
articles.content_orig:
A Canadian family desperately tried to fight off masked intruders at their mansion before a real estate CEO father and his daughters were shot and his wife was attacked with a hammer, according to a report.
MAC Group boss David Morton and his family were attacked at their gated property in Toronto’s upscale Bridle Path neighborhood at around 3:45 a.m. Thursday.
Morton and his daughters, Maggie and Cristina Zohil-Morton, were shot and hit with a hammer as they “tried to fight off” three men wearing hoodies and ski masks, while his wife, Doriana Zohil-Morton, also sustained injuries from the hammer, a source told the Toronto Sun .
Two of the victims suffered “life-altering injuries” and are still in hospital, while the others had non-life-threatening wounds, Toronto Police Service Inspector Kristy Smith said.
Police did not offer descriptions of the suspects but said they had gained access to the six-bedroom residence through a back door.
The seven-bath home is valued at $2.1 million and includes a tennis court, in-ground pool and private gardens to “enhance a luxury lifestyle,” according to an online listing.
The intruders allegedly fled the ritzy nabe in an SUV, officials said.
“There was a violent interaction. There was a demand made for valuables from within the home. Whether or not they escaped with anything is uncertain at this point,” Smith said.
“An affluent area where people would have things that are sought after would be the motivation for this,” she added.
Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow asked anyone with information, including any footage, to come forward and insisted, “violence is not acceptable in our city.”
“I am deeply troubled by the violent home invasion early this morning in the Bridle Path neighborhood. My thoughts are with the family and their loved ones, who are going through something no family should ever have to face. I am praying for their full recovery,” Chow wrote on X.
The family-owned MAC Group is focused on real estate, executive corporate housing, global mobility and Caribbean luxury villas, according to its website.
Morton serves as the CEO, while his wife is the president and their daughter Maggie is listed as an employee. Their other daughter, Cristina, runs Zohil-Morton Law, an immigration law firm.
